Article Title: Congress-NC rift over Vande Mataram: The ghost of 1987 and ‘big brother’ complex
Article Text:
The 1987 ghost: Vande Mataram row and why Omar Abdullah won't let Congress call the shots in J&K.

Venugopal called on allies to honour the wisdom of the freedom fighters

One alliance, two political vocabularies

The alliance and an unequal power equation

What Omar Abdullah had said in 2024

Statehood: Common demand & source of friction

The Rajya Sabha dispute

We felt that the best chance of winning that seat was with the Congress, and they felt otherwise. So be it. Omar Abdullah on RS seat deadlock

The ghost of 1987

1987: The alliance that became a warning

2009-14: History managed, but not erased

The latest Congress-National Conference (NC) clash may have begun with a song, but it is really about something much older: who gets to set the political terms of the alliance in Jammu and Kashmir?CM Omar Abdullah and NC president Farooq Abdullah stood through the full rendition of Vande Mataram on Wednesday at the inaugural International Film Festival in Srinagar. The song was played in its complete six-stanza version, lasting about three minutes and 10 seconds, in line with the Centre's new protocol.This was in sharp contrast with the Congress's stand. Its grand-old party has reaffirmed its 1937 decision to restrict public rendition at party events to the first two stanzas, arguing that the later verses sit uneasily with the pluralist ethos of the freedom movement.Congress general secretary KC Venugopal subsequently said the full version "sits uneasily" with the syncretic and pluralist ethos envisioned by India's freedom fighters and urged allies to stand by the Congress position.The NC was quick to respond, saying the J&K government was only fulfilling its official duty. "After legislative enactment by Parliament, singing Vande Mataram and standing for the song has become a statutory obligation (mandatory legal duty) regardless of the ideological position of any party, group or alliance," said National Conference spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq.The Vande Mataram row is the latest in the list of NC-Congress differences that have surfaced post-election.However, in J&K, the dispute carries an additional historical charge.The NC has spent decades constructing its political identity around a particular proposition: New Delhi can be a partner, but it cannot be the political proprietor of Kashmir's choices.That is where the ghost of 1987 enters.The Vande Mataram dispute has once again exposed an asymmetry that has repeatedly surfaced between the two parties.Congress has to balance its position across India. For Abdullahs' NC, the principal political constituency remains rooted in J&K, where questions of identity, autonomy, federalism and the relationship with New Delhi carry a much more immediate electoral meaning.It is also why the latest row is not an isolated irritant in the alliance.In December 2025, for instance, Omar Abdullah explicitly distanced the NC from Congress's "vote chori" campaign, saying Congress was free to choose its own agenda but that it was not automatically the agenda of the INDIA bloc. With this, Omar tried to assert his party's political autonomy within the alliance.And that has been the recurring pattern.The 2024 assembly election gave the NC-Congress relationship a new lease of life, but it also made the asymmetry between the two parties stark.The alliance crossed the majority mark with 49 seats, with the NC winning 42, Congress six and CPM one. The BJP emerged with 29, PDP three and independents seven.The pre-poll negotiations themselves had not been effortless: the parties agreed that NC would contest 51 seats and Congress 32, while several constituencies remained "friendly contests".The campaign also revealed the limits of joint ownership. Congress and NC leaders did not always campaign together. In Sopore, where the two allies were in a friendly contest, Rahul Gandhi and Omar Abdullah campaigned for their respective candidates separately.During the campaign, Omar Abdullah had publicly noted that Rahul Gandhi should dedicate more campaign time and effort to the Jammu region in addition to Kashmir to maximise electoral impact.Omar himself gave the practical reason for the alliance during the campaign: it was intended to prevent a hung assembly and give voters an alternative.The alliance won the election, and the next question was: what does each side get to claim as its own?The first major post-election rupture came even before the new government had settled in.Omar Abdullah became CM in October 2024, but Congress chose to stay out of his ministry, citing restoration of statehood as its priority. While Congress backed the NC government from outside, its absence highlighted a strategic divide within the alliance. Omar had to engage with Delhi to govern the Union Territory, while Congress sought to pressure the Centre from outside. That difference in approach has repeatedly resurfaced.In July 2025, Congress announced protests in Jammu, Srinagar and Delhi and Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge wrote to PM Narendra Modi seeking legislation to restore J&K's statehood. The NC leadership was irritated because the announcement had not been coordinated with the ruling party. Some NC leaders described Congress's campaign as counterproductive and even as "sabotage" of the government's own efforts.Omar's objection was that Congress had launched the campaign without informing or consulting the NC, leaving its alliance partner caught off guard.The difference is clearer on Article 370 . The NC's 2024 manifesto explicitly called for the restoration of Articles 370 and 35A and reversal of the changes made after August 2019. Congress has similarly opposed the 2019 constitutional changes, but in its recent campaigns placed greater emphasis on the restoration of statehood.Omar reiterated in the J&K assembly in February that his government remained committed to restoring special status, even as statehood remained an immediate demand. By July 2026, he was also linking the restoration of statehood to any future discussion on J&K's earlier constitutional position.This has given the two parties different political priorities.In October 2025, the disagreement moved from ideology to seats. J&K was electing four Rajya Sabha members. The NC, which had emerged as the dominant party in the assembly, initially discussed leaving one seat for Congress.Talks failed.The NC eventually fielded candidates for all four seats after Congress decided not to contest the fourth seat it had been offered, arguing that it was not among the "safe seats" it had sought.Omar's response was strikingly matter-of-fact: "So be it."The NC-Congress disagreement ultimately cost the alliance a clean sweep, with the BJP winning the fourth seat Congress had declined to contest.To understand why the NC may be particularly sensitive to questions of control, one has to go back not merely to 1987 but to 1984.Farooq Abdullah's government was dismissed on July 2, 1984, after 12 NC legislators defected. Ghulam Mohammad Shah, Farooq's brother-in-law and leader of the defecting group, formed the government with Congress support. Contemporary accounts described the episode as a central-government intervention in Kashmir politics; Farooq called the dismissal unconstitutional.For the NC, this was not an abstract constitutional episode. It was a direct lesson in the vulnerability of a regional government to New Delhi's political machinery.Then came 1986.Rajiv Gandhi and Farooq Abdullah reached an agreement that brought the two parties together electorally. A Human Rights Watch report noted that the accord deepened a sense of betrayal among many Kashmiris, who saw Farooq Abdullah compromising with the same Congress party that had pushed him out of office two years earlier.The NC-Congress alliance won 66 of J&K's 76 assembly seats in 1987. But the result was overshadowed by the emergence of the Muslim United Front as an opposition platform, arrests of its candidates and workers, and widespread allegations of electoral rigging. Human Rights Watch later described the election as a turning point that contributed to widespread disillusionment with electoral politics.The significance of 1987 for the NC, therefore, is about the political memory it created. A generation of Kashmiri activists came to believe that the democratic route had been closed to them, a perception that became part of the backdrop to the insurgency that followed.The episode also left an enduring paradox. Congress was simultaneously the NC's electoral partner and a major force at the Centre. That history helps explain the NC's instinct to work with Congress while resisting any perception that Delhi is dictating its regional agenda.That distrust predates the 1980s. In 1953, Sheikh Abdullah was dismissed and arrested after his relationship with the Union government deteriorated. The circumstances were very different, but the political memory was similar: central intervention could reshape J&K's politics. For the NC, unlike many other regional parties, Congress's centralising past is therefore not distant history but part of its own political inheritance.The two parties showed they could overcome that history after the 2008 assembly election. The NC won 28 seats and Congress 17, and the parties formed a coalition government with Omar Abdullah as CM in 2009.But the partnership remained contested. Differences over AFSPA, administrative issues and governance repeatedly surfaced. In 2011, Congress called for consensus on AFSPA while Omar maintained that the state government was an important stakeholder.By 2014, the alliance had run its course and Congress chose to contest the assembly election separately. NC leaders argued that the association with a centrist national party had diluted the party's pro-Valley credentials, with one senior NC leader calling Congress a "very bad alliance partner".The 1987 ghost & real test of allianceWhile 1987 may still shape the NC's political instincts, it would be too simplistic to link every present-day disagreement to that history. The political and constitutional context has changed; however, the experience remains part of the backdrop to the relationship.The lesson for the NC, as we saw in the last election, has not been to avoid Congress, but to work with it where interests converge while retaining its own political space.The Vande Mataram dispute, therefore, is less significant in itself than what it reveals about continuing differences over statehood, Article 370, seat-sharing and the balance between Congress's national strategy and the NC's regional politics.The alliance can survive such differences, but the interesting question now is how durable it will be, which willdepend on how well the two parties manage their competing political priorities.
Article Summary: Congress and National Conference (NC) clash over rendition of Vande Mataram. Row is latest in list of NC-Congress differences that have surfaced post-election. But in J&K, dispute carries an additional historical charge. NC has spent decades constructing political identity around a particular proposition. New Delhi can be a partner, but it cannot be the political proprietor of Kashmir's choices.

Article Title: Brics to kick off with talks to boost multilateralism
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi will host a gala dinner for the leaders participating in the Brics summit on Saturday evening, said govt in an announcement Wednesday. The summit will formally begin earlier in the day with Modi welcoming the leaders of Brics member states at the venue, Bharat Mandapam, and later joining them for a closed session titled Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.India is hosting the 18th Brics summit on Sept 12-13, exactly 20 years after the grouping that counts 11 major emerging economies as members was formalised. After the session, the leaders will witness the Bharat Innovates exhibition at the summit venue, before congregating on the outside lawns for a Brics family photo. This event will be followed by leaders participating in a joint tree plantation.Modi is also expected to have a formal bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping Saturday in which both leaders will look to consolidate gains from the recent uptick in bilateral ties. Xi had last visited India in 2019 for the Mammalapuram informal summit. A formal announcement by Beijing about Xi's visit was still awaited on Wednesday.Modi's bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin is scheduled for Friday. The PM is also expected to have a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. UAE will likely be represented by Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.Bridging bilateral divides over the West Asia situation to secure a unified Brics declaration remains the primary hurdle for India, ahead of the meetings.On Sunday - second day of summit - Modi will welcome leaders of the 10 Brics partner countries, along with other outreach invitees. The leaders will join the final session titled Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.The summit will see a renewed call by Modi for a reinvigorated, inclusive and effective multilateral order at a time when the world is faced with complex challenges. As EAM S Jaishankar had said, Brics needs to commit to a reformed multilateralism that reflects contemporary realities - one where institutions like United Nations, WTO, IMF and World Bank are representative and inclusive.
Article Summary: India is hosting the 18th Brics summit on Sept 12-13, exactly 20 years after the grouping that counts 11 major emerging economies as members was formalised. The summit will formally begin earlier in the day with Modi welcoming the leaders of Brics member states.

Article Title: BJP to celebrate PM birthday, 25 yrs as head of govt
Article Text: NEW DELHI: BJP president Nitin Nabin Wednesday unveiled a month-long calendar of his party's programmes to mark PM Narendra Modi's birthday coupled with the upcoming milestone of his unbroken stint of 25 years as head of govt, with youth at the centre of several events.Sharing details of "Seva Sankalp Abhiyaan", which will start on Modi's 76th birthday on Sept 17, Nabin was dismissive of Rahul Gandhi's Gen Z-centric outreach. "The youth is fully behind Modi," he said. Citing govt programmes like Khelo India, Fit India and Start-Up India among others, he retorted, "Where was Rahul Gandhi then?"

Article Title: Goods train derails in J&K’s Kathua, no injury or damages
Article Text:
Kathua, J&K (ANI photo)

JAMMU: A goods train derailed at Chann Aroria railway station in J&K’s Kathua district on Wednesday morning. Officials said no one was hurt and no damage was incurred in the incident.The derailment occurred around 9.30am when the goods train was heading back after unloading cement, and one of its coaches went off the track in the station’s yard, officials said. A technical team from Kathua rushed to the spot and brought the derailed coach back on track after two hours of efforts.Earlier on July 10, two bogies of a goods train moving from Jammu to Punjab derailed near Lakhanpur in Kathua after debris fell on the tracks following a rain-triggered landslide.
Article Summary: A goods train derailed at Chann Aroria railway station in J&K’s Kathua district on Wednesday morning. Officials said no one was hurt and no damage was incurred in the incident. The derailment occurred around 9.30am when the goods train was heading back after unloading cement.

Article Title: Mahmood Farooqui on Storytelling, Survival and the Human Cost of Imprisonment
Article Text:
Q: Let's start with the art of storytelling.

A:

Q: When you were in Tihar prison, you put together a motley crowd of amateur actors, many of them illiterate, and you had nothing, and yet you brought this about. Let's talk about that.

A:

Q: How does the language of the performance shift?

A:

Mahmood Farooqui is an acclaimed writer and performer known for reviving Dastangoi, the lost art of Urdu storytelling. He has received the Ramnath Goenka Award for Besieged: Voices From Delhi-1857. He has been visiting fellow at the University of Michigan and University of California, Berkeley. Mahmood has co-directed Peepli Live and produced The Great Shamsuddin Family. In this conversation, he discusses 'The Tihar Players'. Excerpts from the interview:When I began work on reviving this or studying about it, I had never seen anyone perform Dastangoi because the last Dastango passed away in 1928. I was very blessed to have the scholarship and the guidance of the great Shamsur Rahman Faruqi, one of the greatest writers, novelists, critics and poets that modern Urdu, or indeed modern India, has produced. But he had also never seen somebody perform. So when we tried to put up the first show, we had the stories, but we had nothing to emulate or no model. So it was really our intuition... that put together the first modern show...And of course, the stories themselves were phenomenal. You know, the story, the fantasies of tricksters and sorcerers, nothing of that kind of imagination and fertility and fecundity has been written anywhere in the world, as far as I know... And then, of course, I started writing my own stories, I started doing workshops. So today, 21 years later, we have. Now the word 'dastan' is back in the currency of our usage in a huge way...We live in a multicultural society. We live in a multilingual society. So any text that I approach, whether I'm working on the Mahabharata or the Ramayana,... many writers in different languages, many literatures have worked on those things. So whenever we present the Mahabharata, people are startled that there are so many versions of the Gita in Urdu or the Mahabharata in Urdu or in Persian, there are so many poems to odes to Lord Krishna, similarly for Ramayana. It's all our legacy. The world of Sanskrit, the world of Persian, the world of Urdu, the world of medieval Hindi. And we bring all that together in the spoken word...I had to do something which in prison terms in India is called mashakkat — rigorous imprisonment. So I went to the education ward and I proposed that I should set up a theatre class... You might think, what is the point of this? You know, my case is more important. I'm very tortured, as everybody in prison is. You know, everybody is suffering. Everybody has got a plethora of problems because there are court cases to deal with, there are families to deal with. There are problems inside prison. There is food, there is medical health. So amongst all those problems and preoccupations, if somebody's saying, come and do theatre with me, it seems a little odd...And then people started getting into it with workshops. When I started, you know, getting them to play out scenes from their own life, from their prison life, then they started enjoying the catharsis... I would consider myself immensely blessed and fortunate that I could see them grow as actors grow in confidence. And it did wonders to their own self esteem. Many of them have benefited from it. Now they're outside, they're working, whether as instructors, public speakers or you know, photographers. And also it did wonders to the atmosphere inside prison because a prison is a very coercive space... We were fighting not so much to be artists, but to restore our own humanity and to find dignity which came to us on stage, which came to us as performers when we saw the gleam in people's eyes, when we saw that for moments when we were doing the Ram Leela, people forgot about everything that was troubling them and they were lost in it.I took a Premchand Munshi called 'Nasha' which we improvised completely. It was a device play. So we brought in a lot of prison lingo...When we did 'Charandas Chor', I tried to retain as much as possible the Chhattisgarhi dialect there because when that dialect was understood by people in Edinburgh, why wouldn't people in Delhi understand it? When I did Molière, I lampoon prison doctors inside... I coined a song about paracetamol. You're dying, you get paracetamol...All the capital and social and cultural capital that I had accumulated outside was of zilch value inside... Nothing really mattered because we had all been reduced to the bare bones of being a human being where we were all being shoved and abused, not just by authoritarian orders or officers, but also inmates. Because always, everywhere, there is a chain of violence that comes from top down, and then you replicate it, then you bully others in turn. When you are stripped of everything that you know, everything that makes your identity, how do you form your identity and where do you stand? How do you say that you know who you are? And I was lucky that my drama class began to believe in me. They began to respect me. They formed a core around me, and I was able to find a place in prison without money, without clout, which is not a mean gift, you know...And when I lived there, I realised people may have committed acts which are illegal, which are maybe reprehensible... Every day they know their families are suffering... There is disgrace, there is suffering, there is deprivation. Sometimes their children have to leave school, sometimes they have to change addresses. Their families sometimes travel hours and upon hours to just come and meet them. So a person's conduct outside does not mean that a person has ceased to be a human being. And second, we send people to prison as punishment. So once a person is inside prison, the person has been punished because a person has been confined. A person has been deprived of their family, of food, of comfort, of a phone, of hugging their children, of hugging their dog, sitting on their chair, having a morning chai. So many everyday things and textures they've already been deprived of when they are inside prison.The law and rules and regulations also follow them inside prison. So people are sent to prison as punishment. But within prison also, they are being punished. Their mulakat might be taken away. Where they are staying might be shifted. Their court cases are inflicting suffering on them. So there is an infinite everyday addition of suffering and punishment and retribution that a person inside is already going through. Regardless of what is happening with their trial, they are suffering humiliation, they are suffering loss of respect, they are suffering insults, they are suffering loss of food, loss of romance, loss of women, loss of hope, loss of time, loss of opportunity. So when you are inside, you're already suffering regardless of the outcome of the case.
Article Summary: Mahmood Farooqui is an acclaimed writer and performer known for reviving Dastangoi. He has received the Ramnath Goenka Award for Besieged: Voices From Delhi-1857. Mahmood has co-directed Peepli Live and produced The Great Shamsuddin Family.

Article Title: "Your biggest responsibility is being a parent": Stephen Curry opens up about raising four children with Ayesha Curry
Article Text:
Stephen Curry opens up.(Image via Getty Images)

Stephen Curry reflects on fatherhood and how much he enjoys rasing his four children with his wife, Ayesha Curry

Stephen Curry reflects on the time he spends with his family as his marriage attracts negative drama

Stephen Curry, the four time NBA champion, might be one of the strongest players and a force to be reckoned with but at home, he has always been a devoted and a present father to the four children he shares with his wife, the popular entrepreneur Ayesha Curry. Amid this, Stephen Curry has reflected on fatherhood.A few years ago, in an interview with POPSUGAR, the Golden State Warriors' star player reflected on fatherhood as he said, "You learn something from them every single day…They give you a reason to wake up in the morning, regardless of whether work is going well or not. Your biggest responsibility, obviously, is being a parent, and it's just so much fun every single day when they change so fast and you're trying to keep up. ”The NBA legend added, “You get to share so many experiences with them and I'm enjoying every minute of it."Stephen Curry continued, "There's something about them that God's put in their life that's going to make them stand out, so embrace whatever that is...As they go through life, that's hopefully what sparks their success."Stephen Curry seems to have a special and an unbreakable bond with each of his four children.Both he and his wife, the popular actress and chef, Ayesha Curry, have always been friendly towards their children and have encouraged them to take up whatever they are interested in, instead of following their father’s path.Stephen Curry seems perfect both on and off the field. While the four time NBA champion has been married to his wife, Ayesha Curry, for over a decade and has been with her since they were young adults, their marriage has always attracted a lot of negative drama.Both Stephen Curry and Ayesha Curry have been mature enough to ignore it as he has even stood up for her to stop the hate she was receiving from fans.In a recent interview, the NBA icon reflected on his personal life as he said, "You rely on family, for sure. Every year has been a learning lesson when it comes to doing the best we can. Quality time is important and that's when you get the most joy. We really try to protect that at all costs."For now, both Stephen Curry and Ayesha Curry have built businesses together and remain committed to providing help to their hometown in Oakland.With just a few more weeks left for the new season to begin, Stephen Curry remains busy with training and recovery.
Article Summary: Stephen Curry reflects on fatherhood and how much he enjoys rasing his four children with his wife, Ayesha Curry. The four time NBA champion has always been a devoted and a present father to the four children. The NBA legend and his wife have always been friendly towards their children and have encouraged them to take up whatever they are interested in.

Article Title: US President Donald Trump drops vehement criticism on Dallas Mavericks’ Luka Doncic trade: “It might go down as the worst trade in the history of sports”
Article Text:
Donald Trump delivers harsh verdict on Luka Doncic trade. Image via: Luke Hales/Getty Images | Brendan SMIALOWSKI/ AFP via Getty Images

Donald Trump delivers harsh verdict on Luka Doncic trade 19 months later

How Luka Doncic's trade changed the Mavericks and the NBA

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Luka Doncic trade is not winding down, as it has found a new critic. The president of the United States, Donald Trump , stopped by the Dallas Mavericks' home arena Wednesday night and told a packed room he still can't make sense of the deal that sent Doncic west.Trump was speaking at American Airlines Center during the Republican National Committee's midterm convention, and basketball wasn't even the point of the night. He brought it up anyway and went on to compare Dallas trading away its franchise star to one of the most infamous sales in baseball history.Nineteen months after the trade went through, Donald Trump stood inside the building where Doncic used to play and admitted the whole thing still baffles him. His remarks came on the opening night of the RNC's two-day midterm convention, the first time the event has been held at the Mavericks' arena. Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the USA" was still fading out as Trump walked onstage around 8:10 p.m.He was upfront about not being a basketball expert. That didn't stop him from delivering a verdict anyway. Trump said, "This is a big Dallas Mavericks team, which is going to be hopefully good.I must tell you, I don't understand the trade. That trade is not, what do I know about basketball? I would say it's not going to go down as the greatest trade in the history of sports. It might go down as the worst trade in the history of sports. "Further, the President went on to compare the Red Sox-New York Yankees wild 1919 Babe Ruth trade, "Babe will always be the worst trade. But is it Luka? Maybe we could redo that trade. I redo deals all the time. We gotta redo that deal. I don't get that deal. Some deals you understand; I understand deals. But that one I didn't quite get."The trade closed on February 2, 2025, and it was bigger than a straight one-for-one swap. It was actually a three-team deal that also pulled in the Utah Jazz. Dallas sent Doncic to Los Angeles and got back Anthony Davis, Max Christie, and a 2029 first-round pick. Nine months later, the Mavericks fired general manager Nico Harrison, the man who built the trade, and handed the front office to Michael Finley and Matt Riccardi.Three months after the trade, Dallas won draft lottery luck and took Cooper Flagg first overall. Flagg started every game he played as a rookie, averaging 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists, and won Rookie of the Year. Davis lasted only 20 games in Dallas before a February 2026 trade sent him to Washington, while Christie stuck around and shot 40.4 percent from three across 77 games. The Mavericks are still in the puzzle and attempting to rebuild the roster.The Mavericks still finished 26-56. Masai Ujiri took over basketball operations in May, hired Mike Schmitz away from Portland, and parted ways with coach Jason Kidd soon after. Dusty May now runs the bench. Doncic, meanwhile, is averaging 31.9 points, 7.8 rebounds, and 8.1 assists across 92 games in Los Angeles, numbers that make Trump's frustration easy to understand, even if the front office saw it differently.Following the trade, there were huge protests by fans, and certainly, it was one of the most talked-about trades in history, as it has also garnered attention from Trump.
Article Summary: The president of the United States, Donald Trump, stopped by the Dallas Mavericks' home arena Wednesday night and told a packed room he still can't make sense of the deal that sent Doncic west. Trump was speaking at American Airlines Center during the Republican National Committee's midterm convention. The Mavericks fired general manager Nico Harrison, the man who built the trade, in May.

Article Title: Dana White’s blunt words on Ilia Topuria reveal what could come next for his UFC return

Ilia Topuria’s UFC comeback may be much closer than expected, and Dana White has now given the clearest update yet. The UFC CEO confirmed that the former lightweight champion is ready to return, despite the serious injuries he suffered in his loss to Justin Gaethje. Topuria’s recovery had already created hope that he could fight again before the end of 2026. White’s latest comments take that optimism a step further. The UFC is ready for him, but his next opponent has not been decided. For now, both Gaethje and Paddy Pimblett remain possible options.Dana White has made it clear that the UFC is not holding Topuria back from competition. Speaking to Jim Rome, White explained that the promotion remains in contact with the former champion and is prepared to move forward when the right fight is available."Our guys are always in touch with them. We don't have him on the schedule right now, but listen, Topuria's ready to fight. We're ready for him."That statement is significant because Topuria’s return looked far less certain immediately after his latest fight.The 29-year-old suffered his first professional loss against Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250. The defeat ended his unbeaten run and came with serious physical damage.Reports indicated fractures to both orbital bones, along with injuries to his nose and foot.Those injuries initially raised the possibility of a lengthy absence. A return in 2027 was even discussed.The recovery process, however, has moved faster than expected.Topuria’s strength and conditioning coach Jesus Gallo previously suggested that the former champion could potentially return before the end of 2026. Topuria has also dropped hints about his next appearance, giving fans more reason to believe his comeback is approaching.White’s latest comments now provide the strongest indication yet that the UFC is preparing for that return.The key point is that Topuria does not have a fight officially booked. That leaves the UFC with an important decision over who should welcome him back.Dana White appears to have two major options in mind for Topuria.One is a rematch with Gaethje. The other is a long-awaited showdown with Paddy Pimblett.When Jim Rome asked White which fight he preferred, the UFC CEO did not commit to either matchup."[Justin Gaethje or Paddy Pimblett?] Both sound good to me. They're both great. We don't lose with either one of those fights. They're both great fights; I don't know."A second fight with Gaethje would give Topuria an immediate chance to respond to the biggest setback of his career. Their first meeting was not decided by a controversial scorecard. Gaethje gradually took control before Topuria’s corner stopped the fight ahead of the fifth round.That makes a rematch easy to understand from a storyline perspective. Topuria would have the opportunity to correct what went wrong and show whether he can handle Gaethje differently the second time.Pimblett offers another kind of attraction.The two lightweight stars have built a heated rivalry over several years. Their relationship has included repeated verbal attacks and confrontations, giving a potential fight plenty of tension before the opening bell.White acknowledged that history while discussing the matchup."They're both great; we don't have anything set… I don't really have the answer to that question. I mean, obviously the rematch with Gaethje is incredible. And a Paddy Pimblett fight is amazing. You know, as bad as those two hate each other."There is also a sporting question surrounding the Gaethje rematch. Topuria lost the lightweight title without successfully defending it, while Gaethje has argued that another contender should have a stronger claim to the next championship opportunity.That could make an immediate rematch difficult to justify from a rankings standpoint.Still, White’s comments show that the idea remains alive.For now, the biggest takeaway is not which opponent Topuria will face. It is that the UFC boss believes the former champion is ready to return.Dana White has effectively moved the conversation forward. Topuria’s comeback is no longer simply being discussed as a future possibility. The UFC is preparing for it, and the next decision could determine whether he returns looking for revenge against Gaethje or settles his long-running rivalry with Pimblett.
Article Summary: Dana White confirms Ilia Topuria is ready to return to the UFC. Former lightweight champion suffered serious injuries in loss to Justin Gaethje. Article Title: Barry Melrose cause of death: How did the former player, coach and ESPN analyst die at 70
Article Text:
Barry Melrose Dies at 70 (Getty Images)

What was Barry Melrose's cause of death?

How did Barry Melrose build his legacy across playing, coaching and broadcasting?

Barry Melrose, one of the most recognizable faces in hockey broadcasting, died Wednesday at the age of 70. His wife, Cindy, confirmed the passing to ESPN, which broke the news to a hockey world that had not forgotten the man who spent decades shaping how fans understood the sport. Melrose had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2023, leading to his retirement from ESPN after nearly 30 years with the network. His death drew immediate tributes from across the NHL, the broadcasting world, and beyond.Barry Melrose died following a battle with Parkinson's disease. The illness had already forced him out of public life two years earlier. When he announced his retirement in October 2023, he said: "I've had over 50 extraordinary years playing, coaching and analyzing the world's greatest game, hockey. It's now time to hang up my skates and focus on my health, my family, including my supportive wife Cindy, and whatever comes next. "ESPN did not formally confirm Parkinson's disease as the official cause of death, but the timeline is clear. The diagnosis came just as the 2023-24 NHL season opened, and he never returned to the desk. When ESPN's Steve Levy announced on the eve of the 2023 Stanley Cup Final that Melrose would not continue their long streak of covering the series together, it led many in the hockey community to suspect something was wrong.That suspicion turned out to be correct.Melrose was 67 when he got the diagnosis. He was gone at 70.Melrose finished his NHL playing career with 10 goals, 33 points, and 728 penalty minutes across 300 regular season games. He suited up for the Winnipeg Jets, Toronto Maple Leafs, and Detroit Red Wings. The stats tell you what kind of player he was: hard-nosed, physical, not there to fill up the scoresheet. What he was building, though, was something harder to quantify.As a coach, he took the Wayne Gretzky-led Kings to the precipice of their first Stanley Cup in 1993 in his first season guiding an NHL team. That run was stunning. Los Angeles lost to the Montreal Canadiens in five games, but the Kings had never been there before, and Melrose had gotten them there in year one. He continued coaching the Kings for two more seasons, finishing both years out of the playoffs with losing records. Just 30 minutes after the Kings fired him in April 1995, Melrose was signed by ESPN to work as a studio analyst during the upcoming NHL playoffs. That timing says a lot about how the network saw him.His television career defined him to a new generation of fans. Known for his sense of humor, his mullet, and his fancy suits, Melrose became a star on ESPN, endearing himself to hockey fans everywhere. He had a way of making the game feel approachable without ever dumbing it down.When asked what he wanted viewers to take away from watching him, he told the Los Angeles Times in 1995: "When [people] watch me on TV, I want them to go, 'Geez, I'd like to go for a beer with Barry Melrose and talk hockey. He seems like he'd be very interesting.'"NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman paid tribute after the news broke.ESPN's John Buccigross wrote: "Barry was my best friend at ESPN. A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core. Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season. Chilling and fitting — the rink was Barry's home. A more beloved ESPN institution there has not been. We love you, Barry. Forever. "
Article Summary: Barry Melrose, one of the most recognizable faces in hockey broadcasting, died Wednesday at the age of 70. Melrose had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2023, leading to his retirement from ESPN after nearly 30 years with the network. The illness had already forced him out of public life two years earlier.

Article Title: Varun Chakravarthy's second act: Why India's mystery spinner still believes he's only halfway through his career
Article Text:
India's Varun Chakaravarthy (Image: IANS)

Learning a new kind of injury

Why shoes matter more than mystery

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the most important trait for a T20 cricketer? Adaptability. Aggression. Consistency. Strategy. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The curiosity beyond cricket

NEW DELHI: For a cricketer who made his international debut at 29, Varun Chakravarthy measures time differently.Now, at 35, he has just lived through a rollercoaster year: a T20 World Cup title on home soil where he finished as India's joint-highest wicket-taker with 14 wickets, an IPL campaign played through hairline fractures in his left hand and toe, and then the first muscle injury of his career that forced him into weeks of rehabilitation.Yet, ask him where he stands in his journey, and his answer is strikingly uncomplicated."At this stage of my career, I still feel I'm in my first half of my career because I started cricket very late. So I still feel there's a long way to go," Chakaravarthy said in an interaction with TimesofIndia.com, facilitated by equipment manufacturer ASICS.It is an outlook that perhaps explains Chakravarthy's unconventional rise better than any statistic. The Tamil Nadu spinner has never been one for grand declarations or five-year plans. In a sport as volatile as T20 cricket, he prefers chasing the next small improvement rather than the next milestone.Now fully recovered from the Grade 2 left hamstring injury he suffered during the England T20I series, Chakravarthy returns just in time for a busy stretch: three T20Is against Afghanistan, a historic one-off international against Japan, and the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, where defending champions India begin directly from the quarterfinals.Until this summer, pain had always arrived the same way for Chakravarthy, through collisions, impact or bad luck.A torn muscle was unfamiliar territory."This is actually my first ever muscle injury. So all of my injuries have been impact injuries and other accidents that have happened on field. The expertise at CoE helped me and people helped me to gain my confidence. Every person working there helped me," he explained.Recovery meant long days at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, where rebuilding confidence became as important as rebuilding strength. The rehabilitation, too, was relentless."Definitely, I spent a lot of time there and did a lot of running and did a lot of strength training, which helped me."For a bowler whose craft depends on rhythm as much as deception, returning isn't simply about being medically fit. It's about trusting the body enough to express the imagination that makes him so difficult to read."Yeah, it will take some time to gain confidence. But once you gain confidence, you just start becoming more expressive and that's how it is," reasoned the 35-year-old.Rather than treating injury lay-offs as wasted time, Chakravarthy sees them as opportunities to work on parts of the game that competition rarely allows."When you're away, you can start sharpening your skills. You can upskill yourself, which you don't get much time to do when you're playing continuously."Mystery spin is often associated with wrists, fingers and release points. Chakravarthy begins somewhere else entirely: the feet.His partnership with ASICS may be commercial, but his relationship with the brand predates the endorsement. He says he had already switched to their shoes around 2022 before formally signing a deal in January 2026.More revealing is how clinically he breaks down footwear."For a bowler, shoes are the biggest equipment they can have. Batters, they have many other equipments, but for a bowler, it's the shoes only," said Varun."As a spinner, your feet start becoming little broader as in it starts changing shape once you pivot because the spinners have to pivot more after landing. So broad shoes in the toe area that is very important," he added.Add a supportive heel counter and lighter weight, he says, and you've got the essentials of a spinner's toolkit.It's the kind of detail that reflects Chakravarthy's evolution from architect to elite cricketer: analytical, process-driven and constantly searching for marginal gains.The Asian Games, which begin on September 19, offer something even ICC events cannot — a sporting village shared with athletes from dozens of disciplines. For Chakravarthy, that might be the biggest attraction."It's my first time in Japan. I've never been to Japan and any games also. So all I've played is ICC tournaments and ACC tournaments," said Chakravarthy, his excitement quite evident in his voice."I'm very much looking forward to meeting other athletes also from other different sports and all those things.""I want to see how a 100-metre athlete prepares himself, how a badminton professional prepares himself or herself," he went on to state.In India's increasingly packed cricket calendar, opportunities for cross-pollination are rare. The Asian Games provide a window into sporting cultures that cricketers seldom experience.That openness may also prove useful on the field. The pitches at Korogi Sports Park are expected to differ from familiar Indian surfaces, and Chakravarthy believes adaptability will define the bowling attack's success more than preconceived plans
Article Summary: Varun Chakaravarthy made his international debut at 29. The 35-year-old has never been one for grand declarations or five-year plans. He says he prefers chasing the next small improvement rather than the next milestone. The Tamil Nadu spinner's partnership with ASICS predates the endorsement.

Noah Lyles wasn’t planning on playing ‘commentator’ ahead of the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship.The reigning men’s Olympic 100m champion had been looking forward to joining the sport’s biggest stars at World Athletics’ new season-ending showpiece in Budapest, until injury forced him to end his season early.In a video call with reporters on Tuesday, Lyles grinned when he was asked a couple of times for his views on some of his rivals who will be in action this weekend. “Shoot, I usually focus more on myself than other people,” Lyles said in response to a question about his American compatriot Kenny Bednarek attempting the sprint double in Budapest. When the very next question was about what impression he had of some of the South African sprinters, the 29-year-old smiled again while going on to say, “I’m not here to be a commentator of sorts today. That’s not really my goal.”And then came a question about 2027. The conversation was about Noah Lyles once again. And the four-time 200m world champion was only too happy to look ahead to what he considers the ‘building blocks’ in his quest to defend his Olympic 100m crown on home soil in Los Angeles.“I am very excited for 2027. It’s going to be a lot of fun,” Lyles said. “2027 is the building block for 2028. And let’s get that plan smooth and polished so that when we go into 2028, we’re just following the blueprint because we know it’s going to work.”Though he sustained his season-ending injury at the US nationals in July, Lyles managed to run two 9.7-second races at the event before the setback, leaving even himself a little ‘shocked’.“I don’t like to put limits on myself,” Lyles said. “In my head, American records definitely come in touching the stars, going after anything and everything. I think I kind of shocked myself a little bit by running those two 9.7s at the nationals because although I was prepared to run fast, I wasn’t prepared to do it then.“So it’s proven to myself that I can run very fast, even though I’m not 100% perfect with my first 30 (metres), which was a super exciting thing. So there’s a lot more to come for 2027 and 2028.”The competitive absence of Lyles is undoubtedly a blow to an event World Athletics has billed as ‘the best of the best’ with a record $10m prize purse on offer. But there’s still a lot on the programme to keep athletics fans hooked, the 1500m race in particular one of the event’s top attractions, seeing as it is set to reignite the rivalry between Great Britain’s Josh Kerr and Norway’s Jakob Ingebrigtsen.Ingebrigtsen’s recent criticism of Kerr for skipping the European Championships last month may well have added a layer of spice to their upcoming showdown. “Always under criticism,” Kerr, who clocked 3:42.66 in the mile at the London Diamond League in July to break Hicham El Guerrouj’s 27-year-old world record, said with a wry chuckle in response to his fierce rival’s comments.“Every person is different, and every athlete is different in the way that they approach the season. For me, the way that I approach it is circling two to four big dates and working my way around those and also to get in and out of a year without massive problems,” added the Scot, who won the 1500m gold at the 2023 world championships in Budapest.
Article Summary: Noah Lyles says he is not planning on playing 'commentator' ahead of the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship. The reigning men's Olympic 100m champion had been looking forward to joining the sport's biggest stars at World Athletics’ new season-ending showpiece.

Article Title: Who are Drew Lock’s parents? Meet Andy and Laura Lock, the family behind the Seattle Seahawks QB
Article Text:
Who are Drew Lock’s parents? Meet Andy and Laura Lock, the family behind the Seattle Seahawks QB(Instagram)

Who are Drew Lock’s parents, Andy and Laura Lock?

How Drew Lock’s parents supported him throughout his NFL journey

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Drew Lock has stepped back into the spotlight for the Seattle Seahawks after Sam Darnold was ruled out with a hip injury during the season opener against the Patriots. Lock entered the game as Seattle’s backup quarterback and took over for Darnold. But behind his long football journey are two people who have been there from the beginning: his parents, Andy and Laura Lock.Both of Drew’s parents had sporting backgrounds of their own, and they played a major role in helping him develop as an athlete and as a person. While Andy had experience as a college football player, Laura was a standout basketball player who later worked in education.Drew was born in Columbia, Missouri, on November 10, 1996, and grew up in Lee’s Summit. He was raised by Andy and Laura on their 10-acre family homestead, where sports became a big part of his childhood.Andy had played offensive tackle for the Missouri Tigers from 1986 to 1989. He went undrafted after college but received an opportunity to attend New York Giants training camp after his playing career at Missouri. His football career did not last long, but he later built a career in business. A LinkedIn profile previously cited in reporting listed Andy as a regional manager with the McCormick and Schmidt’s franchise in Lee’s Summit from 2005.Laura grew up in Centralia, Missouri, and was a star high school basketball player. She later worked as a teacher and school administrator. Her own experience in sports helped her understand the demands placed on a young athlete, although she was also closely involved in Drew’s life away from competition.Andy and Laura met at a bank in Columbia. Laura was working there as a teller when Andy came in to make deposits for a restaurant where he was working after his time with the Giants. Their meeting eventually led to marriage and the birth of Drew and his sister Claire.Laura has recalled how athletic Drew was from a very young age. He played basketball, baseball and other sports while growing up, and his parents encouraged him to develop his abilities without becoming too focused on his own success.Laura was one of Drew’s biggest supporters, particularly when he faced criticism. During the 2020 COVID-19 controversy involving the Denver Broncos, she publicly defended her son and explained that Drew and the quarterback room had asked for permission to watch film at the team facility.Drew later described his mother as a “fiery” person and acknowledged that she would always stand up for him. He also joked about how strongly she reacted when he did not play well.His parents were equally emotional supporters during his college career at Missouri. Laura admitted that watching Drew take hits as a freshman was difficult for her. She recalled sitting in the stands, covering her eyes and hoping he would get back up. After games, Drew would reassure her that he was fine.The quarterback has also spoken about how much it meant to have Andy and Laura attend his games. After one of his early NFL victories, Lock said, “It means the world to me that they end up coming to all these games for me.” He added that they had supported him throughout college and would continue trying to do the same in the NFL.Laura also tried to keep Drew humble as his football career grew. She encouraged him to be thankful for his abilities and to help the people around him rather than boasting about his own achievements.Now, with Lock back on the field for Seattle, his parents remain an important part of the story behind the quarterback. Andy gave him an understanding of the highs and disappointments of football, while Laura provided the constant support and encouragement that followed him from childhood to the NFL.
Article Summary: Drew Lock was born in Columbia, Missouri, on November 10, 1996, and grew up in Lee’s Summit. He was raised by Andy and Laura on their 10-acre family homestead. Andy had experience as a college football player, while Laura was a standout basketball player who later worked in education.

Article Title: 'Scientific evidence backing my case': Anaya Bangar hits back at critics, claims no 'unfair advantage'
Article Text:
File photo/Agencies

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Transgender cricketer Anaya Bangar has responded to criticism over her participation in women’s cricket in Australia, saying she has scientific evidence to show that she does not have an unfair physical advantage.Bangar, the daughter of former India cricketer and ex-batting coach Sanjay Bangar, played age-group men’s cricket for Mumbai before beginning her gender transition in 2022. She underwent gender-affirming surgery in March 2026.The 25-year-old has been cleared by Cricket Australia to play women’s cricket at community level in Australia, subject to its policy requirements.Bangar told the UK-based Daily Mail that she wanted to use the criticism surrounding her eligibility to create more awareness about transgender athletes and the process they go through."I'm willing to take that and basically try to turn that into education and awareness, which I intend to do through my case and many other people out there who have gone through the same process as me and don't have any unfair advantage," she said, as quoted by Daily Mail."I think that's where it all comes down to, and I hope people eventually understand."As part of research at the Manchester University Institute of Sport, Bangar was assessed after more than a year of hormone replacement therapy and testosterone suppression, Daily Mail report said.Researchers looked at her lung capacity, power output and haemoglobin levels and compared the results with those of cisgender female athletes.Bangar said the measurements from the research fell within the range recorded among cisgender female athletes."Whatever data that suggested, it all fell within that range," Bangar said.She said her argument was based on the results of the research rather than her personal views."I'm not talking from personal feelings or opinions. I have actual scientific evidence backing my case. My advocacy in this part is that not all trans women have an unfair advantage. It needs to be assessed on a case-by-case basis, similar to how Cricket Australia has approached my case, and I think that's how it should be worldwide as well."
Article Summary: Anaya Bangar says she has scientific evidence to show she does not have an unfair physical advantage. The 25-year-old has been cleared by Cricket Australia to play women’s cricket at community level in Australia. She underwent gender- affirming surgery in March 2026. Bangar is the daughter of former India cricketer Sanjay Bangar.

The selectors have opted for Yash Thakur as his replacement, handing the Vidarbha pacer another opportunity at international level.Yash Thakur gets another India call-upThe 27-year-old Thakur recently made his T20I debut during India's tour of Zimbabwe in July. Article Title: ‘Dead woman breaks’ 2 FDs of Rs 30 lakh, ex-bank manager, aide arrested in Mumbai
Article Text:
A bank employee can be seen. (AI-generated image used for representational purpose)





MUMBAI: The Central Cyber Police have arrested a private bank’s former Chowpatty branch manager and an employee in connection with an alleged Rs 29.83 lakh fraud in which money was siphoned from the account of a deceased customer after her registered mobile number and email ID were allegedly changed using a forged customer request form.Police arrested former branch head Rahul Panjwani and employee Abhishek Verma on Monday. Another bank employee, Ram Pal, is absconding.The case came to light after the bank received a complaint about unauthorised changes to the mobile number and email ID linked to the account of late Vimla Patil.An internal inquiry found that the details had been changed in July 2025 through a customer request form submitted at the Tardeo branch. The signatures on the form allegedly did not match those in the bank’s records.During the inquiry, Verma allegedly told the bank that Panjwani had instructed him to make the changes. The altered details were then allegedly used to access Patil’s account and prematurely close two fixed deposits worth Rs 14.87 lakh.The proceeds were transferred through RTGS, NEFT, UPI, IMPS and mobile banking to several accounts.Three RTGS transactions of Rs 5 lakh each were allegedly sent to an account in another bank.The transaction trail also showed payments to jewellery outlets. Chimaji Adhav, senior inspector of the Central Cyber police confirmed the arrest.The bank has alleged that Panjwani, Verma and Ram Pal conspired to prepare the customer request form in the name of the deceased customer and forged her signature. Police are probing the alleged conspiracy, money trail and role of the absconding accused.
Article Summary: Police arrested former branch head Rahul Panjwani and employee Abhishek Verma. Another bank employee, Ram Pal, is absconding. Article Title: Great escape: How 2 teens fortuitously dodged Satya Niketan tragedy
Article Text:
On the day of the collapse, Habeeb (L) was visiting his uncle in Zakir Nagar, while Navneet (C) travelled to his native place in Uttar Pradesh





NEW DELHI: For 19-year-old Habeeb Khan and Navneet, being away from their PG accommodation on the day of the building collapse in Satya Niketan proved to be the difference between life and death.Habeeb was visiting his uncle in southeast Delhi’s Zakir Nagar, while Navneet travelled to his native place, Kila Parikshitgarh, in Uttar Pradesh for Janmashtami . Both were expected back in Satya Niketan Sunday, but instead learnt through phone calls and WhatsApp messages that the building they used to stay in had collapsed.Habeeb’s belongings were buried under the debris. Cops from South Campus police station found a bag containing Rs 40,000 in cash and, after verifying his identity, called him and handed over the money. His father later mentioned the incident in a social media post, thanking police.The PG had recently been painted inside and outside, giving it a spanking new appearance, Habeeb said. “It did not look like an old building. Construction work was on for the past 10 days. I used to live on the first floor and could hear the noise and feel the vibrations,” he said.A BA programme student at Motilal Nehru College, Habeeb has been staying at the PG for around a month.The accommodation had a capacity of 16 beds and charged around Rs 16,000 a bed per month, he said, adding that only two beds were empty.With his birthday and a festival falling around the weekend, he decided to spend some time in Zakir Nagar, he said, adding, “I lost some friends to the tragedy.”For Navneet (19), a simple request from his roommate and friend, Arpit Jaj, is the last memory he has of him. “Come soon, Navneet. I want to have cold coffee made by you,” Jaj had told him on the phone a few hours before he died in the collapse. Another close friend, Akshit Yadav, also perished.Navneet was staying in Room No. 302 on the third floor of the PG for around a year. He said the accommodation appeared less cramped than other PGs they had checked out. “This was the only one where we could get a room with a balcony,” he said.Navneet was supposed to return to Satya Niketan with his uncle early Sunday, but the plan fell through. He learnt about the incident from his native place. “At first, I thought a part of the building had collapsed. I did not realise the extent of what had happened,” he said, adding that he didn’t suspect the PG was structurally unsafe.“All my original educational certificates were buried under the debris, along with my clothes and everything else. I want my documents, especially my Class X and XII marksheets,” the second-year BA programme student said.However, returning to the locality is out of the question. “I don’t think I will be able to go back. I don’t think I am in that condition,” Navneet said.
Article Summary: Habeeb was visiting his uncle in southeast Delhi’s Zakir Nagar. Navneet travelled to his native place, Kila Parikshitgarh, in Uttar Pradesh for Janmashtami. Both were expected back in Satya Niketan Sunday, but instead learnt through phone calls and WhatsApp messages.

Durga idol inside Cambridge University museum





KOLKATA: Did you know that a Durga idol has been preserved at the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, University of Cambridge, for nearly a decade? The museum staff call her “The Cambridge Goddess”.The idol was worshipped at the community Durga Puja organised by the Indian Cultural Society (ICS), Cambridge, till it found a permanent home at the Cambridge University museum. ICS is an association largely comprising Bengalis teaching or studying at Cambridge.As ICS enters its 25th year of Durga Puja celebrations, the organisers are trying to collaborate with Cambridge University on another conservation project involving their idol.“Since one of our idols is already being preserved by the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, University of Cambridge, we feel the need to do something similar in this milestone year,” said Nandan Sengupta, one of the Puja organisers who also teaches management at the university.“At that time, the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology showed great interest. It took some time to establish all operational details, including the logistics of transferring the idol safely to the museum.After detailed planning and an operational review, the idol was taken in. It remains there at the museum at the heart of Cambridge," said Sengupta."It makes sense to collaborate with Cambridge University to do something, apart from preserving our protima (idol), that evokes interest among people from all over the world who come to study or teach in Cambridge about Durga Puja, aligning with the Unesco recognition. In our 25th year, we are reminiscing about our journey and achievements that we could be proud of and pass on to the next generation so they can continue maintaining their heritage and culture,” Sengupta aded.10 years ago, ICS members felt the need for a new Durga idol, which got them thinking about what would happen to the old idol.Since there is no provision for “bhasan” or visarjan (immersion) in the UK, immersing the idol in a river would be considered polluting. If permitted, any bhasan would have to be a ritualistic gesture, after which the idol would have to be lifted from the river and disposed of properly.That would have been expensive, and many elderly members would not have been comfortable with the process. The younger members started looking for alternatives.Apart from donating the idol to an upcoming or newly formed Durga Puja committee, another remote option was to approach Cambridge University to check if it would be interested in displaying the idol as part of heritage and cultural preservation.Despite several hindrances, this was the easier part of a two-part job, the second being the disposal of the old idol. Idols are either kept in individuals’ homes or stored in warehouses.“The University of Cambridge, which has seven museums, agreed to keep the idol eternally as a heritage icon. What a relief it was for us,” said Sengupta.“The logistics were not simple, but for a museum it was not much of a challenge. Struck by her gorgeous appearance, visitors want to know more about the culture and heritage that she represents. The museum staff lovingly started calling her ‘The Cambridge Goddess’,” said Sengupta.After the installation of the Cambridge Goddess, Mark Elliott, senior curator for anthropology, wrote to the Puja organisers: “The pratima is a very important addition to the Museum as an example of the devotional tradition in West Bengal and of twenty-first century work by the artists of Kumartuli. Moreover, I think its greatest value for us is to enable us to represent the living South Asian heritage of Cambridge. It is as a Cambridge object, as well as a Kolkatan, Bengali and Hindu one, that I would like it to have an impact on our galleries and our audiences."“Today we have installed Her in the main anthropology gallery, where She will now be on permanent display and accessible to all visitors, particularly members of the Indian Cultural Society and the local South Asian community more generally. I’m delighted to say that she has already made a big impact on our staff and on visitors. I would be happy to welcome you to the Museum to show you myself, but please also feel free to visit, as always, any time the Museum is open. ..”
Article Summary: A Durga idol has been preserved at the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, University of Cambridge, for nearly a decade. The idol was worshipped at the community Durga Puja organised by the Indian Cultural Society (ICS), Cambridge. ICS is an association largely comprising Bengalis teaching or studying at Cambridge.

Article Title: Anthropic researcher who quit over AI safety walked away two months before his stock vested; says: I no longer have anything to gain by…
Article Text:
Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic four months in, two months before his equity vested, saying he no longer had anything to gain from the company's valuation.

Anthropic is heading for one of the biggest IPOs ever, and safety is the sales pitch

Coxon says he never saw Anthropic cut corners. He worries the race will force it.

An Anthropic safety lead replied to the resignation thread and agreed with it

An Anthropic researcher who resigned this week over AI safety fears gave up his entire stake in the company to do it, walking out two months before his equity was due to vest.Jacob Coxon, 27, spent three years doing pretraining research at OpenAI before moving to Anthropic in July. He lasted four months. Staff need six for their stock to vest. His resignation post on X on September 9, now past 130 million views, said neither lab is acting responsibly and that both are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives".Axios first reported the forfeited equity, after Coxon told the outlet on Wednesday that "I no longer have anything to gain by juicing up Anthropic's valuation" and that he left before any of his shares vested. He still holds equity in OpenAI, where his work included GPT-4o.The company is preparing a listing at a reported $2 trillion valuation, built in large part on its reputation as the frontier lab that takes risk seriously. That is what gives the equity detail its weight. Researchers have walked out of rival labs over safety before, usually after their stock vested. Coxon left with nothing, then criticised the valuation he could have profited from.He drew that line carefully in the interview. Anthropic's safety work is sincere, he said, and he has not seen it compromised to outpace competitors. What worries him is pressure over time. Race hard enough and you cut corners, or skip steps in the oversight process. He also described a mood he thinks becomes self-fulfilling, calling it excessive paranoia about OpenAI and about China. Colleagues, he wrote earlier, have started using words like "crunchtime" and "endgame".His most quoted line was about where these decisions are being taken. It is insane, he said, that the work happens on the MacBooks of engineers in San Francisco rather than in a bunker in the desert like the Manhattan Project.Evan Hubinger, who runs alignment stress testing at Anthropic, wrote that he personally puts the odds of AI killing all humans above 10 percent within the decade. He said the company is trying, but has no plan yet for aligning superintelligence and is not clearly on track to find one.Coxon's argument is partly about candour. Executives soften their phrasing for the press, he wrote, then say the same things privately, and the belief that AI could kill everyone by the end of the decade is not a marketing stunt. He also described something that used to be a thought experiment. Models now know when they are being tested, and reason about the fact while it is happening.He pointed to the recent run of cyber incidents at frontier labs, including July's Hugging Face breach, as evidence the risk has left the theoretical stage. Coxon is among more than 1,000 researchers who recently signed a statement calling for governments to coordinate on a way to slow AI development if models start improving on their own. Anthropic has not commented on his departure.
Article Summary: Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic four months in, two months before his equity vested, saying he no longer had anything to gain from the company's valuation. Anthropic is heading for one of the biggest IPOs ever, and safety is the sales pitch. Coxon says he never saw Anthropic cut corners. He worries the race will force it.

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit

Article Title: "Trans women are.....": Clavicular’s viral moment with trans women sparks fresh conversation on internet culture
Article Text:
A viral clip featuring Clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Instead of conflict, the exchange highlights shared influence and mutual awareness. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration rather than ownership.

Clavicular and trans women share a surprising realization about online trends

The video of Clavicular, a short-video producer, is going around the Internet, yet not the reason why. There is no yelling or over-the-top drama. It is a mere, everyday talk that seems almost novel nowadays, in the age of internet, which is overflowing with content. The scene is easy-going, the tone of the narrative is straightforward, and the characters appear more concerned with conversation than combat.The message that is being addressed is the flow of the conversation. It discusses internet culture, the way people communicate with one another and the place of trends. Rather than bringing out a debate, the encounter towards curiosity. It quietly brings attention to something that a lot of people who use the internet notice but don't often say out loud. People in different communities often have a bigger impact on each other than they think.The conversation begins with a confident and lighthearted comment from one of the trans women present. She says, "You know that trans women are like the OG lip masters, right? We are very talented in the program. Like, I do the peptides, I'm on Zeta." Her tone carries a mix of pride and humor, setting a relaxed vibe at the table.Clavicular responds in a way that keeps the mood steady but adds a different angle.He says, "That is funny because you guys were using a lot of the words in like the South Korean subreddits in like 2014." It’s not confrontational. If anything, it feels like an observation. He points to how certain words and ideas may have traveled across different online spaces over time.Another voice joins in and brings the moment full circle. "Guys, we're like the OGs. I saw a couple of posts about that. We're like copying each other." That line hits in a simple but honest way. It reflects something familiar. Online culture is rarely created in isolation. It grows through sharing, borrowing, and sometimes even unknowingly repeating.That's what makes the clip so powerful. It doesn't want to make a point or win an argument. It only shows a group of people talking, listening, and figuring something out together.This moment feels different in a space where viral content often leads to fights. It reminds people that conversations can be calm, thoughtful, and still important. And sometimes, that honest silence is what makes it work.
Article Summary: A viral clip featuring Clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration.
