Article Title: Theatre review: A quietly powerful meditation on love, loss, memory and moving on
Article Text:
Still from the play

Dhoop Ka Ek Tukda

Hindi

Dhoop Ka Ek Tukda





A woman walks onto the stage and sits down on a bench. Every day, she sits there, waiting for a sweet spot of sunlight to hit it. Today was no different. Except today, she had company. After making some small talk and observations, she turns to her invisible companion and begins recounting her past.Director Rajiv Kohli’s, based on acclaimedwriter Nirmal Verma’s short story of the same name, can feel heavy at times, but never exhausting.Through a Virginia Woolf-esque stream-of-consciousness narrative, we understand that the heroine has separated from her husband. And that separation has made her reflect on life and its impermanence with a bittersweet kind of wisdom.Despite the personal tragedy, the protagonist’s interior world is vast, colourful and curious. Sitting on the bench, she ponders over how places like benches and graveyards have no names, like certain buildings do, because it is the people who give character to these inanimate things. Graveyards and benches house no one except the haunting memories of people who have left.The protagonist, years later, still remembers vividly the moment she decided to leave her marriage. She describes it as a loud knock inside her heart that made her sit up in the dead of the night.A loneliness so scary it made her want to run to her parents’ room. But neither that room nor her parents were there.Alone, dejected and immeasurably sad, she sat at her husband’s side of the bed, tracing her fingers over his body. Again, and again, and again. Like she was trying to memorise him but at the same time, also make sense of the stranger who slept soundly as the life they had built together for eight years fell apart. And it is in these moments, the teen lead Sakshi Kumari shines the brightest.Displaying a maturity far beyond her age, the actor takes the audience on an aching, emotional journey of a woman who has loved, lost and is still learning to be open to life without letting her grief turn into bitterness. Such emotional precision is hard to nail in 45 minutes, but Sakshi’s elegance and vulnerability elevate an already fully realised drama. No mean task, that.Keeping the audience engaged while presenting these philosophical musings is a challenge that the trifecta of direction, set design and performance rises to wonderfully. Made up of a wooden bench and a huge tree cut-out with some nice lighting, the small set was tastefully done to contain the writing’s melancholy.At one point in the drama, the character asks the audience, “Why is it that when a building becomes dilapidated, everyone knows about it, that it is no longer fit to live in. But when something like that happens to a relationship, no one seems to care?” And that is the questionwants us to dwell on long after the lights are dimmed and the curtains are drawn.Want us to review your play? Mail us at tims.delhitimes@timesofindia.com
Article Summary: Director Rajiv Kohli’s, based on acclaimedwriter Nirmal Verma’S short story of the same name, can feel heavy at times, but never exhausting. In these moments, the teen lead Sakshi Kumari shines the brightest. Displaying a maturity far beyond her age, the actor takes the audience on an aching, emotional journey.

Article Title: Temple torn down, but Ujjain's Khade Hanuman idol won't move; IIT experts called to solve mystery
Article Text:
An eight-foot Hanuman idol remains in place amid temple demolition for road widening

A temple gone, the idol still standing

Is the idol rooted deeper than it appears?

Where faith meets infrastructure

‘Powers higher than them exist’

The devotees keep coming





UJJAIN: In the heart of Ujjain’s bustling Bada Sarafa market, an eight-foot idol of Khade Hanuman stands under a waterproof tent, surrounded by the broken remains of the temple that once sheltered it.Around it, however, almost everything has moved on.Municipal plans call for a road between Kanthal and Gopal Mandir to be widened from 9 metres to 15 metres ahead of Simhastha 2028. Four religious structures lie along the 450-metre stretch, and the administration says all have agreed to relocate.One Ganesha temple has already been shifted.The Hanuman idol, however, remains where it has stood for generations — and has emerged as the most difficult piece in a road-widening project that was expected to be relatively straightforward.The administration has now made one thing clear: no attempt has so far been made to remove or relocate the idol, either manually or with machinery. Ujjain SDM LN Garg said misleading claims were circulating on social media about repeated attempts to shift it.Instead, officials are turning to engineers and technical experts before taking any step.The question is deceptively simple: how do you move an idol that may be structurally connected to what lies beneath it, without damaging either the idol or the heritage associated with it?The temple structure itself has already been dismantled. Its boundary wall and spire were carefully removed four days ago after the priest and members of local Hindu organisations gathered for a final aarti.The administration had identified a new location near an old water tank at Chhatri Chowk for the idol. According to officials, the priest had consented to the relocation and preparations for a new pedestal were under way based on instructions from the temple’s guruji.But the idol itself has not been touched.Additional municipal commissioner Santosh Tagore, who was at the site along with Garg, said the administration would wait for a technical assessment before deciding what happens next.“For the Hanuman idol, a technical team from SGSITS Indore and IIT is being called in for a proper analysis,” Tagore said, adding that the new site had already been finalised and its pedestal was being prepared.“Nothing further would be attempted until the situation is fully understood,” he said.That caution has changed the character of the dispute. What began as an infrastructure exercise has now become a question of engineering, archaeology, faith and heritage.One theory being examined is that the idol may have been installed using an old interlocking technique, with stones beneath it fitted tightly together.If so, what appears to be an idol standing on a pedestal may in fact be part of a much larger structure beneath the surface.Officials believe a detailed scan of the ground may be required to determine how deep that structure extends and how the idol is connected to it.Archaeologist Raman Solanki, who visited the spot as a curious resident and not in any official capacity, examined the stone at the rear of the idol and identified it as Malwa basalt.He said the idol could potentially be as much as 1,000 years old and possibly date to the Parmar era.Solanki believes that if the stones beneath the idol can be carefully separated, it may be possible to free it without causing extensive damage.That possibility, however, will have to be established through technical examination rather than assumption.For the administration, the road project is tied to preparations for Simhastha 2028, when Ujjain will see a massive influx of pilgrims.The 450-metre stretch is being widened to ease congestion, and officials say development work cannot simply be put aside.At the same time, the administration is now emphasising that development cannot come at the cost of religious sentiment or heritage.Garg said the matter was deeply connected to the faith of devotees and that no decision would be taken without scientific and technical opinions.“While the development works for Simhastha 2028 are important, preserving Ujjain's faith and heritage is equally significant,” he said.The administration, he added, would seek a consensus-based solution through dialogue with devotees, saints and experts.For temple priest Mahesh Bairagi, the uncertainty surrounding the idol has reinforced his belief that its relocation should not have been treated as a routine municipal exercise.“The setback makes it clear that no real preparation had gone into planning the idol’s move. Authorities should understand that powers higher than them exist,” he said.Religious organisations have also urged caution.Vishwa Hindu Parishad's Khagendra Bhargava said old temples and idols should be relocated only when absolutely unavoidable, and that the complete traditional and administrative process must be followed with due respect.The question of the idol's age, if established by experts, could make the issue even more sensitive.Meanwhile, the most visible part of the story is not the road, the engineers or the municipal files.It is the devotees.Even with the temple structure partly dismantled, worship has continued. Bairagi performs the morning puja amid the remains, blessing visitors with the ritual whisk as he has done before.Queues of devotees continue to form for darshan of what many now regard as a miracle — an idol that remains standing amid a road project designed to make everything around it move.Members of Hindu organisations have maintained a presence around the site, while police personnel remain stationed nearby. At times, slogans have been raised against the municipal corporation's handling of the matter.For now, the administration has chosen caution over force.The road may need to become 15 metres wide for Simhastha 2028. The temple structure has already made way.But the eight-foot Hanuman remains exactly where generations of devotees have known him to be.And before anyone decides where he should go next, experts will first have to establish what, exactly, lies beneath his feet.
Article Summary: The Hanuman idol has emerged as the most difficult piece in a road-widening project that was expected to be relatively straightforward. The administration has now made one thing clear: no attempt has so far been made to remove or relocate the idol, either manually or with machinery.

Article Title: Theatre review: 500 years later, The Queen still knows how to play the game
Article Text:
The Queen, a historical drama set in 1585, explores themes of power and betrayal. Queen Durga navigates palace politics after her husband remarries a younger woman. The play balances political intrigue with sharp wit and moments of humor. Puja Sarup delivers a commanding performance as the astute Queen Durga. This production offers a compelling look at family dynamics and shifting loyalties.

The Queen

Genre:

Historical drama

Rating: 3.5 stars

Cast: Puja Sarup, Mukul Chadda, Sharvari Deshpande, Rohit Mehra/ Dheer Hira

Director: Daniel Owen Dsouza

Duration: 80 minutes

Language: English

Should you watch this play?

The Queen will be staged in Mumbai next month. (October 7 and 8, NCPA)





Who would have thought that the story of a royal family in the fictional 16th-century kingdom of Banasvan could feel relatable 500 years later? Yet, that is precisely the strength of The Queen, written by Aditya Rawal and directed by Daniel Owen D'Souza. At its heart, this is a story about power, shifting loyalties, betrayal and the fear of becoming irrelevant; themes that transcend time and place.The drawback is that the brisk 80-minute runtime, at times works against it. There is plenty happening with palace politics, family tensions, shifting alliances and the threat of betrayal - but some relationships and emotional beats could have benefited from more room to develop. At times, the pace feels a little hurried, with certain moments passing before they have a chance to fully register.Set in 1585, the play follows Queen Durga, who is moved to the west wing of the palace after her husband, King Amar, marries a younger woman. Suddenly pushed to the margins, Durga finds herself grappling with her fading relevance, while worrying about her son, Prince Veer, and the king’s increasingly dangerous ties with the emperor.But this is no helpless queen. Brilliant, perceptive and politically astute, Durga knows that one wrong move could cost not just the kingdom, but the lives of everyone she loves.Aditya's writing is top-notch, with razor-sharp wit, nuanced characters and dialogues that land beautifully. The best part is perhaps the way it balances the weight of palace politics with humour and sarcasm. Durga, a compelling protagonist quickly senses her son’s affair with her maid Laila, even as she remains alert to the machinations of her adversaries. Beneath the humour is an ever-present sense of danger, making the audience constantly wonder who will betray whom. Puja Sarup as Queen Durga, brings authority, vulnerability and quiet menace to the role. Sharvari Deshpande as Laila is equally impressive, particularly with her vocal prowess, which comes as a pleasant surprise. Mukul Chadda as King Amar and Rohit Mehra as Prince Veer add depth to the complicated family dynamics with their performances.The production is visually appealing, with set designer Shaira Kapoor creating a world that transports the audience into the corner bedroom of the old Queen of Banasvan. The music by Khamosh Shah, with lyrics by Raghav Dutt, complements the narrative without overpowering it. Despite its occasional rush, The Queen manages to pack intrigue, humour and family drama into a compact running time, with Puja’s performance giving the play its strongest anchor.Yes, especially if you enjoy sharply written historical dramas with, dark humour and a strong central female character.
Article Summary: The Queen, a historical drama set in 1585, explores themes of power and betrayal. Queen Durga navigates palace politics after her husband remarries a younger woman. The play balances political intrigue with sharp wit and moments of humor. Puja Sarup delivers a commanding performance as the astuteQueen Durga.

Article Title: Theatre Review: Siachen explores the psychological cost of survival as soldiers battle isolation and fear
Article Text:
The dramatic play Siachen immerses audiences in the harrowing world of soldiers facing relentless extreme conditions and deep-seated psychological trauma. Isolation and a constant undercurrent of fear challenge their mental resilience atop the unforgiving icy terrain. Through the poignant writing of Aditya Rawal, the audience is taken on a journey into the human mind grappling with prolonged hardship, while Makarand Deshpande's direction skillfully unveils the core vulnerabilities of the characters.

Siachen (Drama)

Critic's rating: 3.5 stars

Cast: Zahan Kapoor, Niketan Sharma, Ashish Bhatt, Jatin Sarin, Chitransh Pawar, Rohit Mehra, Nitin Passi Mannu, Seerat Mast and Shruti Jolly

Director: Makarand Deshpande

Duration: 1 hour 15 minutes

Language: Hindi

Should you watch it?





When a small stage inside an auditorium can transport you to a glacial peak more than 20,000 feet above sea level, to an Indian military post in the unforgiving terrain of Siachen, you know the play is doing something right.Siachen, written by Aditya Rawal and directed by Makarand Deshpande, is an intense survival drama that takes you far beyond the physical battle against the elements and into the fragile human mind.The play opens with the death of one of four soldiers (Nitin Passi Mannu) stationed at a remote military post after a deadly avalanche cuts off all communication with the base camp. Stranded on the ice-covered peak, Lieutenant Tanmay Bose (Zahan Kapoor), Lance Naik Anthony D'Souza (Aashish Bhatt) and Subedar Shabbir Naqvi (Niketan Sharma) are left to fend for themselves.Their ordeal is almost unimaginable. The transmitter is dead, there is no safe route down to the base camp and the brutal cold is an enemy that never lets up. Though the post has enough food, survival is about much more than food. As the days stretch into an uncertain wait, the soldiers battle hallucinations, isolation, fear and the psychological trauma of watching their comrades die. The mountain slowly begins to test not just their physical endurance but their grip on reality.And this is where Aditya’s writing truly shines. He explores what prolonged isolation at one of the most inhospitable places on earth can do to the human psyche. The physical toll is immense, but the mental toll is far greater. Aditya takes each character towards his psychological breaking point, allowing their vulnerabilities, fears and contradictions to emerge organically. The sharp, dark humour threaded through the narrative also offers moments of relief without diluting the gravity of their situation.With Makarand at the helm, the nuances of these characters come alive. His direction ensures that we don't merely watch these soldiers struggle, we begin to care about them, flaws and all. The claustrophobic setting becomes a character in itself, constantly looming over them.The performances are uniformly strong. Zahan, as Tanmay, the highest-ranking officer at the post, brings a restrained intensity to the role. His understated performance works particularly well as he attempts to shoulder the responsibility of keeping the others together. Niketan is particularly impressive, portraying a man desperately trying to hold the team together even as circumstances threaten to pull them apart. Aashish is equally convincing , bringing warmth and vulnerability to his character.Jatin Sarin, as the Pakistani local, is another standout, adding yet another layer to a narrative where notions of enemy and ally become complicated by the sheer force of survival.What makes Siachen especially compelling is the way it reminds us that on a glacier, even after a ceasefire, humans are not entirely in control of their fate. The weather becomes the ultimate arbitrator -- indifferent to borders, uniforms, rank or politics. At an altitude where every breath, every movement and every decision comes at a cost, nature has the final word on life and death.Where the play falters slightly is in its pacing. The prolonged stretches of psychological unraveling, while effective in establishing the soldiers’ state of mind, occasionally feel repetitive and could have been tightened. Some of the hallucination-driven sequences also verge on feeling overly theatrical, taking away from the otherwise grounded realism of the narrative. At times, the intensity is also pushed a little too hard, when the quieter moments are actually more powerful.Siachen is ultimately not just a play about soldiers stationed on the world’s highest battlefield. It is a powerful exploration of camaraderie, isolation, fear, resilience and the extraordinary lengths human beings will go to in order to survive.​ And for 90 minutes, that little auditorium stage becomes the frozen, unforgiving expanse of Siachen, and you feel the cold.Absolutely. Siachen is gripping, thought-provoking and emotionally powerful​ and goes beyond the familiar war narrative to explore the psychological cost of isolation, survival and uncertainty.
Article Summary: Siachen is an intense survival drama that takes you far beyond the physical battle against the elements and into the fragile human mind. The physical toll is immense, but the mental toll is far greater. The sharp, dark humour threaded through the narrative also offers moments of relief without diluting the gravity of their situation.

Article Title: 8 boys 'illegally' held, rights body seeks FIR on Pune CP, 14 cops
Article Text:
The minors were allegedly illegally detained for five days and assaulted after being paraded in public (AI-generated image used for representational purpose)

Right body flags public parading of detained minors in Pune





MUMBAI: The state human rights commission, MSHRC, has directed the DGP to register an FIR against over 15 Pune police officers, ranging from the commissioner to a constable, for allegedly illegally detaining eight minors in a murder case for five days and assaulting them in public.A senior Pune police officer declined to comment, stating he had not seen the order, reports Vijay V Singh.MSHRC has also recommended invoking provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act against the officers concerned, as four of the minors belonged to the SC/ST communities. The directive follows a report from an MSHRC fact-finding team, which included a special IGP.The minors, some of whom surrendered before the police in a murder case, were allegedly kept in illegal custody in a police station for five days and subjected to assault after being paraded in public. When one of their family members challenged the detention, the minors were produced before the juvenile justice board.MSHRC chairperson Justice (retd) A M Badar, and members Justice (retd) Swapna Joshi and IPS (retd) Sanjay Kumar, noted that “both parts of the report of fact-finding inquiry along with its annexures be treated as the FIR as envisaged by Section 173 of BNSS, 2023 and for completion of consequential investigation expeditiously.”Earlier, MSHRC had formed a fact-finding team consisting of Datta Karale (special inspector general of police), Vijay Kedar (registrar) and Viswas Pandhare (SP) posted at MSHRC to look into the incident.The committee recorded the statements of the affected parties, examined the spot, CCTV footage and the police case diary to conclude that human rights violations were committed.
Article Summary: The state human rights commission, MSHRC, has directed the DGP to register an FIR against over 15 Pune police officers. The officers are accused of illegally detaining eight minors in a murder case for five days and assaulting them in public. Four of the minors belonged to the SC/ST communities.

Article Title: Khalapur temple theft: Video shows masked man stealing silver Padukas; 2 arrested in Pune
Article Text:
he accused stole silver Charan Paduka from Shree Swami Samarth temple on September 2





NAVI MUMBAI: The Khalapur police probing the theft case wherein a masked man had decamped with a pair of silver toe-knob sandals (Charan Paduka) representing divine footprints offered at Shree Swami Samarth temple in Khalapur city on September 2, have arrested the acccused thief and his aide by tracking them to Pune on Monday.Pradeep Rayannavar, senior inspector of Khalapur informed that, the arrested accused are Mahendrasingh Rathod, 45, who hails from Rajasthan and Ravi Soni, 32, who hails from UP and is a history-sheeter as a theft case is registered against him in Pune.Both were presently residing in Chikhali, Pune district.On September 2, the temple trustee Deepak Bodarde, 68, lodged a complaint of theft of silver Padukas from the temple.When the CCTV footage of the temple premises was checked, it was seen that a masked man wearing a hat and attired in white Kurta-Payjama entering the temple around 7.30am.He goes to the first floor of the temple where the silver Padukas were kept in front of the idol of Shree Swami Samarth.By pretending to offer prayers, he picked up the Padukas and hid them inside his Kurta and exited the temple.Inspector Rayannavar said," The theft was committed when the temple priest had gone to his room near the temple.Upon checking the CCTV footage of the roads near the temple, it was seen that two masked men on a bike were loitering near the temple and conducted a reece before committing the theft.""Considering the religious sentiments of the devotees, Raigad SP forms a special police team to detect the case at the earliest. Subsequently, the CCTV footage along the escape route of the thieves were scanned. The bike used in the crime did not have a registration number plate," Rayannavar added.He further said, "However, using technical expertise, intelligence inputs and footages of CCTV camera along the highways, the thieves on bike were tracked and apprehended from Chikhali in Pune district. We have seized from them the stolen Padukas and the bike used in the crime. On Monday, the acccused were produced before the Khalapur JMFC court that remanded them to police custody till Friday."
Article Summary: A pair of silver toe-knob sandals (Charan Paduka) representing divine footprints offered at Shree Swami Samarth temple in Khalapur city were stolen on September 2. The accused thief and his aide were arrested by tracking them to Pune on Monday.

Article Title: Cop dies by suicide at Navi Mumbai lodge, names ex-DCP, ACP and head clerk in note alleging harassment
Article Text:
The deceased identified as Pandurang Nimba Patil, a resident of Airoli.





NAVI MUMBAI: A 55-year-old Assistant Sub-Inspector (ASI) with the Navi Mumbai Police allegedly died by suicide at a lodge in Airoli on Saturday evening.The deceased, identified as Pandurang Nimba Patil, a resident of Airoli, had recorded a video before taking the drastic step and posted it on social media.In the video, he alleged that he was compelled to end his life due to harassment by a former DCP, an ACP, and a head clerk.ASI Patil also left behind a nine-page suicide note accusing former DCP (Headquarters) Sanjay Patil, ACP Girish Thakare, and administrative head clerk Jayu Ahire of driving him to take the extreme step by allegedly harassing him while assigning official duties.ACP (Rabale Division) Rahul Dhas said, "ASI Patil had checked into Sachi Lodging and Boarding on Saturday at 4.40 pm. Around 7.30 pm, when the housekeeping staff went to his room, he did not respond, and the door was locked from inside. The lodge manager opened the door with a master key and found ASI Patil hanging from a ceiling fan hook. The lodge manager informed the Rabale MIDC police. ASI Patil was rushed to NMMC Hospital in Vashi, where he was declared brought dead. Prima facie, an accidental death case will be registered at the Rabale MIDC police station."
Article Summary: Pandurang Nimba Patil, a 55-year-old Assistant Sub-Inspector (ASI) with the Navi Mumbai Police, allegedly died by suicide at a lodge in Airoli on Saturday evening. He recorded a video before taking the drastic step and posted it on social media. In the video, he alleged that he was compelled to end his life due to harassment by a former DCP, an ACP, and a head clerk.
